#10800. New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck

The rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

These challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

To address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait

Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information quickly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely new photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever new capabilities are needed.

The problem is especially important for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light

The research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a new design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

Using the new CRIT structure, the researchers showed that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape

The researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also showed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

The design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several important capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems

Professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies."

Co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We plan to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation."

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is currently conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

Dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

Materials provided by Seoul National University College of Engineering. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10799. Former senator whose arrest went viral on YouTube wins another election

A former senator in Minnesota has been elected to a city council a year after a conviction on two felony burglary counts and being highlighted by a true crime YouTuber.

Back in August 2025, the true-crime YouTube channel Midwest Safety highlighted the story of Nicole Mitchell, the former Minnesota state senator.

Mitchell had been arrested by police back in 2024 after gaining entry to her stepmother’s house. The politician stated that she was there to retrieve belongings owned by her recently deceased dad because her stepmother “wouldn’t talk to me anymore.”

However, she then changed her story during a court trial, saying she wanted to check on the well-being of her stepmother. Mitchell was found guilty after a three-hour hearing and sentenced to 180 days in county jail. She was released in January 2026 after an early release appeal.

Mitchell initially said that she wouldn’t resign from her post, but ultimately did. Yet, she has now gotten back into politics.

The former state senator has been elected to a position on the Woodbury City Council, which has come under some scrutiny given her previous conviction.

As per local reports, the Minnesota Department of Corrections website previously stated that “if you are convicted of a felony you lose the right to hold public office until court-ordered discharge from probation or the end of your sentence.”

Some noted that was changed in 2023, but others have argued that the change only surrodned the ability to vote for a candidate, not actually run for office.

That would be for voting only. Below FAQ is the current Dept of Corrections website. pic.twitter.com/HEvXTBS3js

“She is the first convicted felon to be elected in Minnesota. She is currently on probation. Yes, she was “featured” on Midwest Safety,” the YouTube channel posted on November 11.

Terafab’s procurement team reportedly has already been to Japan, asking some toolmakers to deliver within months.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk’s Terafab, a joint venture of Tesla and SpaceX, has informally told equipment makers it is seeking to produce 1 million wafers per month after 2032, according to Financial News. About 70% of this output, or 700,000 wafers, is planned to go to memory, with more than 300,000 going to logic chips. Terafab’s procurement team has already visited Japan to ask some local toolmakers for delivery within months. The memory allotment would rival Samsung’s estimated DRAM production capacity if it were all of that type.

Samsung’s DRAM capacity was estimated last year at 650,000–700,000 wafers a month, while SK hynix is reportedly at about 550,000, with about 1 million a goal by 2030. The comparison has to be taken in context, as Terafab’s 700,000 measures all of its expected memory output, which could be NAND or DRAM, while the Samsung and SK hynix figures measure only DRAM. As it is, the memory portion alone would be 3.5 times the reported 200,000 at SK hynix’s Wuxi fab in China.

Many in the industry were skeptical when Musk announced the plans in March, but orders are now leading more companies to see a real business opportunity. The timeline is aggressive, as it usually takes three years or more to get from planning to volume at a leading-edge fab, and Terafab is targeting volume production in the second half of 2028. Procurement officials from the company reportedly visited Japan earlier this month to meet local suppliers and to work on details on bringing in equipment, with some suppliers asked to deliver within a few months.

The Elec also reports that Terafab representatives visited booths of about 10 Korean materials, parts, and equipment firms at SEMICON West, with some NDAs signed.

Logic chips are one thing — Jiji Press reports Terafab is working with Intel to adopt its 2nm and 1.4nm processes — but memory is another, and it’s not clear what type of memory is on the docket. Technical help from a Taiwanese company is under consideration for memory, but no partner has been named, leaving 70% of the planned wafers without a disclosed process technology.

Memory production tends to split between DRAM and NAND flash, the latter for non-volatile storage. A Tesla job listing for a Terafab Memory Process Integration Engineer, reported in August, covers end-to-end DRAM process integration and DRAM node development, and supports emerging memories such as MRAM, RRAM, and 3D DRAM. Terafab hasn’t said how its DRAM would be divided among products like HBM and LPDDR, both useful for AI and both mentioned in its job postings, or whether it expects to make and stack the DRAM itself or package chips it brings in.

Building a cutting-edge logic fab on U.S. soil is its own challenge, and Tesla and SpaceX lack chip-manufacturing experience. Even Musk, on a SpaceX call last month, called Terafab’s dates “very aggressive” and said he put “big error bars” on the timeline. The first SRAM test chip is targeted for around May or June 2027 at the Austin research facility.

How TSMC might fit in remains open. TSMC says any fab with its involvement has to be run by TSMC, while Musk said his own companies would build and operate Terafab, a scenario which could leave TSMC as a space tenant. At least the spending plans are known: $16.8 billion for the first phase in Grimes County, Texas, with total investment of up to $119 billion if later phases proceed. A pilot plant could be completed as early as July 2027.

#10795. Toyota is bringing a kei truck to America that only goes 25mph

Toyota is bringing a tiny kei truck to America in 2027 that’s only 11 feet long and has a top speed of 25mph.

Whether you’ve traveled to Japan or played Forza Horizon 6, you’ll likely have seen your fair share of kei trucks. These little vehicles are known for their small size and ability to squeeze into tight spaces with very little problem. They’re both practical for those with minimal space and, well, they’re also rather adorable.

Now, Toyota is bringing this pint-sized approach to the US with a new kei truck model that will be released in the US next year.

Announced on November 10, the KEI-01 measures just over 11 feet long and less than five feet wide. The miniature pickup also comes with a 660cc three-cylinder engine, selectable four-wheel drive, an enclosed cabin, and a cargo bed with three folding sides.

Despite its small size, the truck can carry up to 600 pounds and is capable of towing small trailers/equpment. Inside, drivers get heating, air conditioning, sliding and reclining seats, and storage behind the seats for tools and other gear. Oh, and it also retains its signature right-hand-drive layout.

There is just one catch, though: the KEI-01 tops out at just 25mph. It’s not exactly the fastest truck on the market, but Toyota says the little truck has mainly been designed for use on farms, university campuses, and businesses.

If you’re hoping to buy your own tiny kei truck, you’ll have to wait, as Toyota will initially only sell it to businesses and organizations through selected dealers. However, the Japanese car company has said it may open sales to everyone else later if there’s enough demand.

#10794. MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond quickly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

"The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

The study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

Many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

Silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

At the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

The unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

In a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

The MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way

Reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

Each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

"We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent

Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

The researchers now plan to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

"This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

The Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Adam Zewe. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10790. This company wants to pay you over $100,000 to play GTA 6

A company is offering the chance to earn up to $120,000 by playing GTA 6, with an additional $15,000 up for grabs if they complete the job.

With Rockstar’s long-awaited sequel launching on November 19, millions of players are preparing to lose countless hours exploring Vice City and the state of Leonida.

But while most will have to fit their gaming sessions around work, one lucky applicant could actually get paid a six-figure sum to play it.

Kalshi, an American prediction market platform that allows users to trade on the outcomes of real-world events, is hiring a GTA VI Researcher to investigate the game’s economy and its impact on the real world.

According to the official job listing, the successful applicant will begin playing GTA 6 at midnight on November 19, streaming their entire playthrough on Twitch or YouTube.

They’ll be tasked with finding the most effective ways to make money in-game, analysing Leonida’s economy, and publishing weekly research reports.

The role also involves investigating the game’s real-world impact, including how many people call in sick on launch day and how much productivity is lost.

“We’re looking for someone whose parents said video games would never pay the bills. They were wrong, and you can tell them we said so,” the listing reads.

Kalshi is offering a fixed fee of between $100,000 and $120,000, plus an additional $15,000 upon completion. However, there are some requirements.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old, have 10 or more years of gaming experience, and at least three years of streaming experience. They’ll also need their own streaming channel and equipment, including a reliable internet connection.

Fortunately, Kalshi isn’t expecting anyone to play GTA 6 nonstop, with the listing confirming that breaks and sleep are allowed.

#10789. A 10-Point Checklist for Legacy Application Modernization

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Legacy applications often support critical business operations, but keeping them running can become increasingly difficult. Outdated infrastructure, growing technical debt, security vulnerabilities, and limited integration capabilities can make these systems expensive to maintain and harder to adapt to changing business needs.

Modernizing them involves more than upgrading technology. You need to understand what the existing application does, identify which components need improvement, and manage the transition without disrupting essential operations.

This 10-point legacy application modernization checklist walks you through the process, from assessing your existing systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, testing applications, and measuring results.

Legacy application modernization is the process of updating existing software applications, their architecture, infrastructure, or underlying technologies to meet current business and technical requirements.

Depending on the application's condition, modernization may involve moving it to a new platform, improving its code, redesigning its architecture, or replacing it with a new solution.

The goal is to improve performance, security, scalability, maintainability, and the application's ability to support future business requirements.

Modernization isn't necessarily the same as cloud migration. Moving an application from on-premises infrastructure to the cloud changes where it runs, but it may leave its underlying architecture and technical limitations unchanged.

An organization can modernize an application without moving it to the cloud or combine both approaches as part of a larger transformation.

Use this checklist to track the ten essential steps involved in modernizing legacy applications.

1. Define modernization goals: Identify business problems and establish measurable success criteria.

2. Assess existing applications: Review infrastructure, technical debt, code quality, and performance limitations.

3. Map application dependencies: Document critical workflows, integrations, and business rules.

4. Choose a modernization strategy: Select an approach based on business value, cost, complexity, and risk.

5. Develop a roadmap and budget: Prioritize activities, estimate costs, assign responsibilities, and establish milestones.

6. Plan architecture and security: Design the target environment and address security, compliance, and availability requirements.

7. Prepare data migration: Plan data transfer, integration changes, and validation procedures.

8. Modernize incrementally: Validate the approach with a pilot and implement changes in manageable phases.

9. Test and deploy: Verify functionality, performance, security, and data integrity before production rollout.

10. Monitor and optimize: Measure results, support users, and continuously improve the modernized application.

Let's examine what each step involves and how to determine whether you're ready to proceed.

Before selecting technologies or planning development work, identify what the modernization initiative needs to achieve.

Clear business objectives help prioritize investments, guide technical decisions, and establish whether the project delivers meaningful improvements.

Start by examining the problems affecting your application's performance, reliability, or business value.

For example, a legacy order management system might still process transactions reliably but require extensive manual work whenever the business adds a new sales channel.

In this situation, improving integration capabilities may be more valuable than replacing the entire application.

An application's age alone doesn't justify a major technology investment. Whether legacy modernization makes sense for your business depends on the problems the existing system creates, the cost of maintaining it, and whether smaller improvements could resolve those issues.

Once you've identified the problems, translate them into measurable objectives.

If slow performance is the primary concern, establish a target for response times or transaction processing speed. If maintenance expenses are rising, determine what reduction in operating costs would justify the investment.

Relevant key performance indicators (KPIs) may include:

These baseline measurements will help determine whether the changes deliver the expected results.

Completion check: You have a documented business case identifying the problems to address, expected outcomes, measurable KPIs, and stakeholders responsible for approving success.

A legacy application assessment provides a clear picture of your current technology environment.

Without this assessment, teams may underestimate project complexity, overlook critical components, or choose a modernization approach that doesn't address the application's actual limitations.

Begin by creating an inventory of your applications and their supporting technologies.

Document each application's purpose, business owner, primary users, operating environment, programming languages, frameworks, databases, and infrastructure requirements.

Also identify software versions, third-party dependencies, licensing restrictions, and components approaching or past their end-of-support dates.

If your organization operates several legacy applications, use a consistent assessment framework. This makes it easier to compare their business importance, technical condition, and modernization urgency.

Review the application's codebase to identify issues that make maintenance and development difficult.

Look for tightly coupled components, duplicated logic, outdated libraries, insufficient automated tests, and undocumented configurations.

Pay particular attention to areas where small modifications regularly cause unexpected problems elsewhere in the system.

For example, if payment processing, inventory management, and customer records share tightly connected code, modifying one function could require extensive testing across the entire application.

Your infrastructure assessment should also cover hardware limitations, database compatibility, backup capabilities, operating systems, and unsupported dependencies.

Analyze how the application performs during normal operations and periods of increased demand.

Review response times, database queries, resource utilization, transaction volumes, and recurring failures.

Existing monitoring data and incident records can reveal problems that aren't immediately visible during routine use.

Determine whether performance limitations originate from inefficient application code, infrastructure capacity, database design, or external dependencies.

This distinction matters because adding computing resources won't necessarily resolve problems caused by poor application logic.

Completion check: You have an application inventory and technical assessment report documenting major components, technical debt, operational risks, and performance limitations.

Legacy applications rarely operate independently. They exchange data with other systems, support interconnected business processes, and often contain business rules that aren't fully documented.

Understanding these dependencies is essential because changing one component can affect several other applications or workflows.

Document the processes that rely on the application, including the steps users follow, the data they need, and the expected outcomes.

Work with business users, application owners, operations teams, and developers familiar with the system.

Identify processes that cannot tolerate significant interruption, such as payment processing, order fulfillment, customer authentication, or financial reporting.

Don't overlook activities that happen less frequently. Month-end financial reports, annual calculations, and scheduled data exchanges may depend on functionality that isn't exercised during everyday operations.

Map how the application communicates with databases, APIs, third-party services, and other internal systems.

Include scheduled jobs, file transfers, message queues, authentication services, and reporting tools.

Some legacy applications contain years of accumulated business logic.

Rules for pricing, approvals, calculations, or customer eligibility may exist only in source code, database procedures, or undocumented workflows.

Identify these rules before modifying the underlying implementation.

Where possible, create automated tests that capture existing expected behavior. These tests can help verify that the modernized application preserves required functionality.

Completion check: Critical workflows, system dependencies, integrations, and business rules are documented and reviewed by the relevant business and technical owners.

The appropriate modernization strategy depends on the application's technical condition, business importance, budget, and future requirements.

Not every application needs to be rebuilt. Some systems require targeted improvements, while others may be better replaced or retired.

Common legacy application modernization strategies include:

Different applications within the same organization may require different approaches.

Evaluate each option against your technical constraints and business requirements.

Consider implementation effort, expected benefits, ongoing maintenance costs, required expertise, and potential disruption.

For example, replatforming may be suitable for an application that operates reliably but depends on aging infrastructure. Rearchitecting may be necessary when tightly coupled components prevent independent updates or scaling.

A complete rebuild requires particular caution. Recreating undocumented functionality can be expensive, and important business rules may be lost if the existing system hasn't been thoroughly assessed.

The right strategy should solve the identified problems without introducing unnecessary cost or complexity.

Completion check: Each application has a selected modernization strategy, documented rationale, estimated effort, and an approved decision on whether to modernize, retain, replace, or retire it.

Once you've selected a modernization approach, convert it into an actionable plan.

Your roadmap should establish what will change, in what order, who will be responsible, and how progress will be evaluated.

Prioritize modernization work according to business value, technical complexity, urgency, and dependencies.

Applications with unsupported components or significant security risks may require early attention. However, starting with the most complex application isn't always the best choice.

A smaller, lower-risk application can provide an opportunity to validate tools, workflows, and team capabilities before modernizing more critical systems.

Dependencies also affect the sequence. For example, a shared authentication service may need to be updated before applications that rely on it can be migrated.

Prepare a budget covering the full modernization process rather than development alone.

Compare upfront implementation expenses with expected operating costs over time.

A modernization approach with a lower initial cost may still require significant ongoing maintenance.

Allow contingency for unexpected issues, particularly when legacy documentation is incomplete or system dependencies remain uncertain.

Divide the project into phases with defined deliverables and approval requirements.

Assign responsible owners for architecture, development, security, data migration, testing, and business acceptance.

Establish how project risks will be reported and who can approve changes to scope, budget, or deployment schedules.

Keep the roadmap adaptable. Findings from pilot implementations or migration rehearsals may require changes to the original plan.

Completion check: Your modernization roadmap includes prioritized activities, estimated costs, responsible owners, dependencies, milestones, and approval checkpoints.

The target architecture determines how the modernized application will operate, scale, integrate with other systems, and remain maintainable.

Security and compliance requirements should be incorporated into the design from the beginning.

Choose an architecture that fits the application's actual requirements.

Possible approaches include a modular monolith, service-oriented architecture, microservices, or event-driven components.

Microservices aren't automatically the best option. Although they allow independent deployment and scaling of components, they also introduce complexity in communication, monitoring, deployment, and data management.

For smaller applications or tightly integrated business processes, a well-structured modular architecture may be easier to maintain.

Document architectural decisions covering application components, data storage, interfaces, infrastructure requirements, and operational responsibilities.

Identify security weaknesses that should be resolved during modernization.

Review authentication, authorization, encryption, secrets management, logging, and access to sensitive information.

Evaluate third-party dependencies and establish processes for vulnerability scanning, patching, and security testing.

Regulatory and contractual requirements should also influence the target design.

Security controls should be applied throughout development and deployment rather than added shortly before release.

Define how the application will remain available and recover from failures.

Establish recovery time objectives (RTOs) and recovery point objectives (RPOs) based on business requirements.

Plan backup procedures, restoration testing, appropriate redundancy, and monitoring for critical components.

Validate that the target environment can support the required availability and recovery objectives.

Completion check: The target architecture has documented design decisions, security controls, compliance requirements, availability objectives, and recovery procedures.

Data migration is one of the most sensitive stages of legacy application modernization.

Legacy databases may contain inconsistent records, outdated formats, duplicated information, or relationships that newer systems handle differently.

A migration strategy needs to explain how data will be transferred, validated, and made available without compromising business operations.

Begin by reviewing the quality and structure of existing data.

Identify missing values, duplicate records, inconsistent formats, obsolete fields, and relationships that could create migration problems.

Document how existing data structures correspond to the target system.

For example, a legacy customer database might store contact details in a single field, while the new application requires separate fields for email addresses and phone numbers.

The migration process needs defined transformation rules to handle these differences.

Determine which records must be migrated, archived, retained for compliance, or excluded.

Choose a migration approach based on data volume, application availability requirements, and acceptable downtime.

Depending on the system, this may involve a scheduled migration during a maintenance window, staged transfers, or synchronization between old and new environments.

Identify integrations that will need modification.

Where applications exchange information through APIs, files, or messaging systems, verify that the modernized implementation supports the required data formats and business behavior.

If the legacy and modernized applications will operate simultaneously, define how data updates will be synchronized between them.

Test the migration process using representative datasets before transferring production data.

Validate record counts, field values, relationships, and critical business calculations.

For sensitive or business-critical information, use appropriate reconciliation methods, including integrity checks where applicable.

Document how inconsistencies will be identified and resolved.

Also establish what happens if migration fails or the application needs to return to its previous environment.

Completion check: Data mapping rules are approved, migration rehearsals have been completed, and reconciliation procedures can verify data accuracy.

Modernizing an entire application in a single major release can increase project risk, particularly when the system supports critical business operations.

An incremental approach allows teams to validate decisions, identify problems earlier, and limit the impact of failures.

Select a manageable component or workload to validate your modernization approach.

The pilot should test an important assumption, such as whether the target platform supports the application, whether a legacy integration can be replaced, or whether an architectural change improves performance.

Define success criteria before implementation.

A useful pilot should provide evidence that the approach is technically feasible and that the team can manage its operational requirements.

Use the findings to improve estimates, identify missing skills, and refine the broader implementation plan.

Divide the application into manageable migration or development units where its architecture allows.

One approach is the Strangler Fig pattern, which gradually replaces legacy functionality while the remaining parts of the original application continue operating.

For example, an organization might modernize customer notifications first, followed by reporting and then core transaction processing.

This can reduce the risks associated with replacing an entire system at once.

However, incremental modernization also requires careful coordination. Temporary integrations, duplicated components, and parallel systems can introduce complexity.

Each phase should have defined boundaries, validation requirements, and completion criteria.

Establish repeatable processes for developing, testing, and deploying application changes.

Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines can automate builds, execute tests, and promote approved changes through environments.

Use version control, consistent configuration management, and infrastructure as code where appropriate.

Include security and quality checks in the delivery process to reduce the risk of introducing defects during frequent releases.

Completion check: The pilot has validated the selected approach, implementation is divided into manageable phases, and repeatable build, test, and deployment processes are established.

Modernization isn't complete when the new application runs successfully in a development environment.

It must perform the required business functions, communicate correctly with connected systems, and meet operational expectations before production rollout.

Develop a testing plan based on the application's critical workflows and identified risks.

Automate repeatable tests where practical, especially for critical business processes.

Compare results against the performance baselines and acceptance criteria established earlier.

Business users should verify that the modernized application supports their actual workflows.

User acceptance testing (UAT) should include routine operations, exception handling, reporting requirements, and tasks that depend on specialized business knowledge.

Use representative migrated data during testing.

Confirm that critical records, calculations, and reports remain accurate after the transition.

Resolve issues affecting essential operations before approving production deployment.

Prepare a documented deployment plan outlining the sequence of activities, responsible teams, communication channels, and expected service interruptions.

Choose a deployment method appropriate for the application, such as a phased rollout, canary release, or scheduled cutover.

Establish measurable conditions that would stop deployment or trigger a rollback.

Rollback planning must account for data changes made after cutover. Restoring an earlier application version doesn't automatically restore database consistency, especially if new transactions have already been processed.

Rehearse deployment and recovery procedures in a suitable non-production environment.

Completion check: Required tests have passed, business owners have approved acceptance criteria, and deployment, cutover, and recovery procedures have been validated.

The initial deployment marks the beginning of ongoing operation rather than the end of modernization.

The application needs continued monitoring and maintenance to ensure that expected improvements are sustained.

Compare post-modernization results against the baseline established at the beginning of the project.

Track metrics linked to your business objectives, such as application availability, maintenance costs, response times, deployment frequency, security vulnerabilities, and user satisfaction.

Use monitoring tools, logs, traces, and alerts to identify problems that may not be visible through basic availability checks.

Review performance after deployment and at agreed intervals to determine whether the modernization initiative is meeting its objectives.

Technical improvements may introduce changes to established workflows.

Provide relevant training, updated documentation, and support resources for users and operational teams.

Ensure that administrators and developers understand the new architecture, deployment processes, monitoring tools, and incident response procedures.

Collect user feedback to identify usability issues or missing functionality.

Use production data and operational feedback to guide further improvements.

Optimization may involve updating dependencies, improving database queries, adjusting infrastructure capacity, strengthening security controls, or simplifying application components.

Once replacement functionality is stable and approved, begin decommissioning components that are no longer needed.

Before retirement, confirm that dependent applications have been migrated, necessary records are retained, and archival or compliance obligations have been met.

Removing unused infrastructure and software can reduce maintenance costs and unnecessary security exposure.

Completion check: Monitoring and support responsibilities are established, modernization KPIs are reviewed, and unused legacy components have an approved retirement plan.

Organizations without the internal resources to manage legacy modernization may need support from an external software development company.

Depending on the project, a development partner can assist with application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, system integration, data migration, and implementation.

Companies offering custom software development and application modernization services include:

Idea Maker: Provides custom software development and legacy application modernization services, including application assessments, code refactoring, architecture redesign, and cloud migration.

ScienceSoft: Offers custom software development, legacy software modernization, application reengineering, cloud migration, and system integration services.

Itransition: Provides custom application development, legacy application modernization, system integration, software migration, and post-modernization support.

Simform: Offers digital product engineering, software modernization, cloud and platform engineering, and data integration services.

These are examples of providers rather than a ranked comparison.

When evaluating a development partner, consider their experience with your existing technology stack, ability to handle complex integrations, approach to data security, and experience delivering projects with similar requirements.

Ask prospective providers how they assess legacy systems, manage migration risks, preserve critical business logic, and validate application functionality before deployment.

The main steps are defining business goals, assessing existing applications, mapping dependencies, choosing a modernization strategy, developing a roadmap, designing the target architecture, planning data migration, implementing changes, testing and deploying, and continuously optimizing the application.

The exact sequence may vary depending on the application's complexity and business requirements.

Start by evaluating the application's business value, technical condition, dependencies, and future requirements.

Rehosting or replatforming may be sufficient when the application functions well and infrastructure is the primary concern.

Refactoring or rearchitecting may be necessary when code quality or architectural limitations affect maintainability and scalability.

Rebuilding or replacing becomes an option when the existing implementation no longer meets business needs or would be too costly to maintain.

Compare expected benefits, implementation costs, risks, and ongoing maintenance requirements before making a decision.

Common risks include undocumented dependencies, data loss or corruption, unexpected downtime, security vulnerabilities, integration failures, and loss of essential business functionality.

Projects may also experience delays or budget overruns when technical complexity is underestimated.

These risks can be reduced through early assessment, phased implementation, migration rehearsals, comprehensive testing, and validated recovery procedures.

The timeline depends on the application's size, architecture, technical debt, data complexity, integrations, and selected modernization approach.

A limited rehosting or refactoring project generally requires less effort than rebuilding a large application or modernizing several interconnected systems.

A reliable estimate requires an initial technical assessment. A pilot or proof of concept can help validate assumptions about implementation effort and potential challenges.

Measure success against the business and technical objectives established before implementation.

Relevant indicators include application performance, availability, maintenance costs, security improvements, deployment speed, and user satisfaction.

For example, if reducing maintenance effort was the primary goal, lower support costs and faster resolution of application issues may be more meaningful than infrastructure performance alone.

Modernization success should be evaluated over time rather than only immediately after deployment.

Legacy application modernization works best when it follows a structured plan based on business needs and the realities of existing technology.

The ten steps in this checklist cover the key decisions and activities involved, from assessing legacy systems and selecting a modernization strategy to migrating data, validating functionality, and maintaining the resulting application.

Careful dependency mapping, realistic planning, incremental implementation, and thorough testing help reduce risks throughout the transition.

Start by assessing your existing applications and defining what modernization needs to achieve. Those findings will help you identify which systems deserve attention, where to invest resources, and how to approach modernization without introducing unnecessary complexity.

#10788. Going deep on local AI performance benchmarking with Apple’s Mac Studio with M5 Ultra taking on Nvidia DGX Spark

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Is a Mac Studio a better investment than a DGX Spark?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Apple’s updated Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra SoC has already proven itself as one of the most powerful systems around, thanks to its 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU with Neural Accelerators for the matrix math operations that drive AI compute. Beyond that raw power, options for up to 512GB of unified memory have many local AI enthusiasts lining up for the 13 to 15 weeks it’ll take for Apple to ship one right now.

But is our tested Mac Studio config worth a whopping $12,300 or more for those folks? We already tested the maxed-out M5 Ultra chip with the popular Qwen 3.8 27B in our initial review, but that compact dense model doesn’t come anywhere close to exercising 256GB of memory. We wanted to fill that pool to the brim with cutting-edge large models like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash.

We also have some new benchmarks at our disposal to see how the Mac Studio stacks up in agentic tasks on the GPU side in the wake of our review of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. So there's much to dig into.

We started our more detailed local AI testing with Artificial Analysis' AgentPerf-Local benchmark. This test plays back recorded inference traces with certain models across a range of agentic AI workloads to gauge performance. Artificial Analysis provides a full breakdown of this workload, but the bulk of its work takes place in prompt processing rather than token generation. As a result, it should favor systems with lots of raw compute, which both GB10 and the M5 Ultra have at their disposal.

The M5 Ultra's 80-core GPU dwarfs GB10's 48 Blackwell SMs at a high level. Even without detailed info on clocks, it would be extremely difficult for GB10 to outgun the M5 Ultra in this test. And the Mac's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth gives it just over four times as much decode bandwidth as GB10's 273 GB/s. But as our past tests have shown, raw specs aren't as important as delivered performance with AI. Delivered performance can vary greatly from paper specs.

We continued to use the dense Qwen 3.8 27B for this test. We used llama.cpp as our inference backend on both the Mac Studio and a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 box, which is nearly identical to the DGX Spark. We further enabled Qwen 3.8 27B’s native multi-token prediction (MTP) support for a decode speed boost on both platforms.

Versus a single DGX Spark-like system, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio finishes this agentic test in just under half the time, an extremely impressive result. One might think this is a silly comparison given the imbalance in compute resources and memory bandwidth between these two systems, but the cost of a single 4TB Dell Pro Precision GB10, like the one we tested, is now a whopping $10K, so comparing it to the $12K Mac Studio head-to-head isn’t actually that far-fetched.

Because AgentPerf-Local performs a fixed amount of work on every system, we can also directly compare power efficiency between platforms by recording the wall power consumed by a single Spark and the Mac Studio and converting it to task energy in kilojoules.

At least with llama.cpp, the Mac Studio not only finishes the AgentPerf-Local test much faster than the DGX Spark, but it also consumes less task energy overall — about 16% less. A different inference engine might produce a more favorable result for the Spark-like system, but apples-to-apples, this test looks fantastic for the Mac Studio.

We can multiply both task time and energy consumed (in kilojoules) together to arrive at the energy-delay product (EDP) for each system. A lower EDP wraps up a fast time to completion and a low task energy into a single comparable figure for efficiency.

The Mac Studio’s EDP is under half that of the DGX Spark in this test, once again indicating its impressive efficiency and performance with this dense model and workload.

Of course, Qwen 3.8 27B doesn’t need 256GB (or even 128GB) of RAM to do its thing. To really stretch the legs of the Mac Studio, we chose two larger open models that are near the top of capability benchmarks right now: GLM-5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017.

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio can natively fit quantized versions of these models (a four-bit quantization in the case of GLM 5.3 and a two-bit quantization courtesy of Unsloth for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) in its 256GB of RAM, but there’s no way even those quantizations will fit on a single 128GB DGX Spark.

That’s where the clustering capability of Nvidia’s platform comes in. We’ve already seen how pairing up Sparks can scale up one’s local inference capacity, and that capability is critical when evaluating them against a Mac Studio like this.

But the rapidly rising prices of GB10 systems have frustrated our value analysis during the course of this testing. For just one example, Lenovo set all of its ThinkStation PGX systems to a “coming soon” status during our tests. And as we’ve already mentioned, the Dell Pro Precision GB10s we’re clustering here are an eye-popping $10K each. We have no reason to believe the rest of the GB10 systems on the market will be that much cheaper once this current volatility shakes out.

No matter how you slice it, getting even a pair of DGX Sparks with 4TB SSDs is going to end up costing quite a bit more than this single Mac Studio, even if $20K for a dual-Dell cluster is at the top end of the market. $15K or more is a relatively more reasonable benchmark, but even then, that’s 25% more money than a single M5 Ultra Studio.

We don't yet have end-to-end agentic tests for these larger models, but directionally, we can still consider prompt processing and decode performance to see which of these systems would deliver faster agentic turnaround.

Because of the limited choice of compatible inference engines for Apple Silicon, we have to use llama.cpp for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. Worse, the Mac Studio can't hold both the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 model weights and the DSpark speculative decoding model required to boost token output even with a two-bit quantization, so we’re forced to leave performance on the table.

In contrast, the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash serving recipe for our Spark cluster can take advantage of DSpark speculative decoding and the TensorFold inference engine, which can deliver higher performance than llama.cpp.

Even with MLX support, llama.cpp performance with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the Mac Studio is pokey next to the DGX Spark cluster. Between its slower prompt processing speed and unaugmented decoding, it would end up at a disadvantage in agentic work with this model.

The community two-Spark serving recipe from Mia’s AI Lab with TensorFold is a major asset for owners of those systems, even accounting for the bit of extra work involved in setting up and managing a Spark cluster.

Where the Mac running llama.cpp needs anywhere from 10 to 25 minutes to digest the longest context lengths we tested for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the Spark cluster needs under five minutes at most to do the same jobs with this recipe — and the TensorFold inference engine is much faster on the decode side, too. If you want to run this model locally, a pair of Sparks is the clear winner right now.

With DeepSeek out of the way, let’s consider GLM 5.3 Flash, another leading open model for local intelligence. Because MTP with GLM 5.3 Flash doesn't require a separate drafting model, we can give it a decode boost on the Mac Studio without the memory headroom issues we saw with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. For our Spark cluster, we chose to run GLM 5.3 Flash using a recipe cooked up by Mia's AI Lab.

GLM 5.3 Flash runs much better on llama.cpp than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash does, but even so, the DGX Spark cluster delivers much faster prompt processing times across the board. The M5 Ultra's memory bandwidth advantage means the Mac is delivering higher tokens per second on the decode side, but it’s likely that any agentic turn would still finish faster on the Spark cluster.

Because a TensorFold serving recipe is available for GLM 5.3 Flash on Apple Silicon, however, we can see just how much extra performance is available from an MLX-specific four-bit model quantization and a theoretically higher-performance inference engine.

This serving recipe turbocharges the Mac Studio’s performance compared to llama.cpp. Prompt processing times with TensorFold get much closer to those of the Spark cluster, and decode throughput is a startling three times faster, on average.

We expect (and can only hope) that improved inference engine support and serving recipes for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 on the M5 Ultra will arrive in time as community members unleash their coding agents on this hardware, because the performance potential is clearly there for Apple Silicon.

A single M5 Ultra Mac Studio can deliver incredible local AI performance and power efficiency versus a single DGX Spark when all the puzzle pieces fall into place. And that's not as absurd a comparison as it might seem.

Prices for unified memory systems are ballooning to the point that a single Dell Pro Precision GB10 system with a 4TB SSD is now over $10K, closing in on the $12K-ish price of the Mac Studio configuration that we tested. We expect those trends will only continue as the RAM and NAND supply crunch becomes more acute.

But our broader experience shows that the M5 Ultra's impressive performance isn't assured from every model and inference engine, especially from the bigger and highly intelligent models you'll want to put in 256GB of RAM.

This Mac's prompt processing speeds can really rip with llama.cpp and smaller models like Qwen 3.8 27B, but you really want to ensure that you have a higher-performance serving recipe at your disposal for bigger models like GLM 5.3 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017. The TensorFold engine runs GLM 5.3 Flash incredibly well, but it doesn’t support DeepSeek at all yet.

As we emphasized in our review of the M4 Max Mac Studio, memory bandwidth is just one factor in AI inference performance. You need to take the entire hardware-software stack into account in order to wholly judge the performance and model compatibility available from these extremely pricey unified memory setups.

Even as Apple closes the performance shortfalls of its hardware for AI inference, development and support around the MLX stack has a ways to go before it catches up with the maturity and performance, as well as the model and inference engine options, available on Nvidia hardware.

The enduring value of the DGX Spark platform beyond its raw performance and scalability is that the breadth and velocity of community software development and support around the platform has gotten to the point that you're virtually assured of a way to run a hot new model soon after its weights hit Hugging Face (at least assuming you have enough Sparks to cluster to provide the memory capacity necessary).

That assurance of community software support and ongoing development, along with the DRAM and NAND supply crunches, means high demand and ever higher prices for 128GB GB10 boxes. Two such Sparks with 4TB drives will run you an eye-watering $15K to $20K+, depending on the partner system and storage configuration you choose. And those prices are likely to continue rising, making a single Mac Studio a potentially appealing option as long as Apple doesn’t jack up its prices for these systems in turn.

If strong local AI performance is just one thing you need from a personal workstation, and you also want one of the world's fastest CPUs and a powerful GPU for general-purpose work in one well-rounded, efficient, and quiet compact chassis, the Mac Studio is a remarkable system.

If you can wait for software to catch up to this system’s incredible performance potential for local AI and don’t mind the possibility of narrower model and inference engine support compared to a DGX Spark setup, get in line, as lead times for these systems stretch into February 2027 as of this writing.

But if you're thinking about dropping well over $10K specifically for the purpose of building a local AI inference setup right now, perhaps for yourself or a small office, clustering a pair of Sparks gets you both the memory capacity and compute horsepower you need with the robust software support and broad model compatibility you’d expect for that outlay to be worthwhile. Those assurances may be worth the lower raw performance potential of such a cluster compared to the Mac Studio.

As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

#10787. World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World

Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an important objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero

To make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

"This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

That capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

Materials provided by Aalto University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10785. GTA 6 almost banned in Korea after government officials got to play it early

Grand Theft Auto 6 was almost denied a rating in South Korea, as officials asked to play the game early and see some parts of the map.

With November 19 getting closer and closer, Grand Theft Auto fans from around the world will soon finally get to play GTA 6. However, if you’re in South Korea, that opportunity was almost taken away from players.

As per a report from Inven Global, Rockstar Games’ newest title “came close” to not receiving a rating classification from officials. According to the report, an initial review of the game ended in a three-three between giving GTA 6 an ‘adults only’ rating and not rating it at all.

This review took place in early September, with requests being made to Rockstar so that officials could see parts of the game early and then vote again.

Initially, there were concerns about sexual scenes being out of context and “far too much genital exposure,” rather than the violence or crime side of GTA.

On top of that, security concerns about leaks meant that a playable build was not available to officials until the end of September, hence a delay in handing out a rating to the game.

As per Inven, officials also noted that the map is “so vast” that they had to make multiple requests to Rockstar to point out specific areas around any exposed characters. However, they found that the player “could not engage in any sexual interaction.”

Upon a later review, one member of the committee noted that: “It appears that they intentionally covered genital exposure in explicitly sexual scenes, while allowing exposure in background settings.”

Officials added that it would be a “massive controversy” if they refused to rate the game – which would effectively ban it from being released in Korea – as they’d be the only country to do so.

Fans in Japan and Australia have flagged concerns about those versions potentially being censored, seeing as there is a notable difference in the size of their game files compared to everywhere else.

The preload period for GTA 6 is open to everyone at this point now, but it has caused some disruption for select internet providers in the UK.

#10781. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected

A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially important because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

The researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

By contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
